title: The Art of Talking to AI — Prompting Basics

scenes.narration: Welcome to Nabulines Academy. You've got your Claude account, you've seen Artifacts in action. Now let's talk about the skill that separates beginners from builders: how to actually talk to AI. This isn't about magic words or tricks. It's about being clear, specific, and giving Claude what it needs to help you. By the end of this lesson, you'll have three simple patterns you can use every single time you ask Claude for something. Let's go.

visual.title: The Art of Talking to AI
visual.subtitle: Prompting Basics — Ch0-L4

scenes.narration: First, let's talk about what a prompt actually is. A prompt is just the message you send to Claude — the question, the request, the instruction. Think of it like this: Claude is incredibly smart, but it can't read your mind. If you say "make me a website," Claude has to guess. What kind of website? For who? What should it look like? The more you guess, the more you get something random. But if you're specific — if you say exactly what you want — Claude can build exactly that. So prompting is really just being a good communicator. You're not coding yet. You're describing what you need in plain English. And the better you describe it, the better the result.

visual.title: What is a prompt?
bullets: The message you send to Claude
Claude can't read your mind — be specific

scenes.narration: Here are the three patterns that will change everything for you. Pattern one: Context, Goal, Constraints. Always tell Claude three things. Context: what's the situation? Who is this for? Goal: what do you want? Be specific. Constraints: any limits or requirements? Like "keep it under 100 words" or "use only HTML and CSS." Pattern two: Show, don't just tell. If you want something that looks a certain way, describe it visually. Or better yet, paste an example and say "like this, but for my topic." Pattern three: Iterate. Your first prompt won't be perfect. That's fine. Ask Claude to refine it. Say "make the colors softer" or "add a contact form." Treat it like a conversation, not a one-shot command. These three patterns work for everything — a landing page, a script, a lesson plan, anything.

Let's see what this looks like in practice. Here's a vague prompt: "Make me a website." Claude will do something, but it's a coin flip whether it's useful. Now watch what happens when we apply the patterns. Context: I'm a freelance photographer. Goal: I need a simple portfolio page to show my work. Constraints: One page, clean design, a grid of six photos, and a contact button at the bottom. Now Claude knows exactly what to build. Let's add pattern two — show, don't tell. I'll say: "Make it look modern and minimal, like Apple's product pages — lots of white space, big images." Now Claude has a visual reference. And pattern three: after Claude builds it, I'll say "Can you make the photo grid three columns instead of two?" or "Add my Instagram link next to the contact button." See how we're steering the result step by step? That's the art of prompting.

visual.code:
// Vague prompt (bad):
"Make me a website."

// Specific prompt (good):
"Context: I'm a freelance photographer.
Goal: Build a simple one-page portfolio to showcase my work.
Constraints:
- One page only
- Clean, minimal design (like Apple product pages)
- Grid of 6 photos
- Contact button at the bottom

After you build it, I'll ask you to refine the layout."

scenes.narration: Here's the mistake everyone makes at first: they think prompting is about finding the perfect magic sentence. It's not. It's about clarity and iteration. Your first try will be rough. That's normal. You'll ask Claude for something, look at the result, and realize you forgot to mention the color scheme or the font size. That's fine — just tell Claude to fix it. The best prompters aren't the ones who write perfect prompts on the first try. They're the ones who know how to steer the conversation. They say "a little bigger," "more playful," "add a section for testimonials." They treat Claude like a collaborator, not a vending machine. And that's the mindset shift: you're not trying to trick the AI into doing what you want. You're having a conversation with a really smart assistant who needs clear instructions.

visual.title: The Real Secret
bullets: First try will be rough (that's normal)
Steer the conversation step by step
Claude is a collaborator, not a vending machine

scenes.narration: One more thing before we wrap: always ask Claude to explain. If you don't understand something in the code it wrote, just say "Explain this line to me like I'm five." Claude will break it down. If something doesn't work, say "This button isn't clickable — why?" Claude will debug it with you. You're not expected to know everything. You're expected to ask good questions. And that's a skill you'll use forever — not just with AI, but with every tool, every person, every project. Asking clear questions is how you learn fast.

visual.title: Always Ask Claude to Explain
bullets: Something broken? Ask Claude to debug.

scenes.narration: Alright, you now know the three patterns that will make every conversation with Claude better: Context, Goal, Constraints. Show, don't just tell. And Iterate — refine as you go. Your exercise is to take the vague prompt "make me a website" and rewrite it using these patterns. Be specific. Add context. Add constraints. Make it something Claude can actually build. Do that, and you're ready for the next lesson, where we'll use these prompting skills to build your first real page in Artifacts. See you there.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the Context-Goal-Constraints pattern?
Why is 'make me a website' a bad prompt?
options: It's vague — Claude has to guess what you want
You need to write code first

quiz.q: What should you do if your first prompt doesn't give you exactly what you want?
options: Iterate — refine it step by step in conversation

exercise:
Rewrite this vague prompt into a specific, context-rich prompt using the three patterns:

Vague: "Make me a website."

Your rewrite should include:
- Context (who you are, what the site is for)
- Goal (what you want the site to do)
- Constraints (design style, number of sections, any specific features)
- Optionally: a visual reference ("like X website")

Paste your rewritten prompt into Claude and see what it builds. Then practice iterating — ask Claude to refine one thing about the result.
